1.pericope_label: The word of the Lord which came to Jeremiah the prophet against the Gentiles; Against Egypt, against the army of Pharaoh–necho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah. Order ye the buckler and shield, and draw near to battle. Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen, and stand forth with your helmets; furbish the spears, and put on the brigandines. Wherefore have I seen them dismayed and turned away back? and their mighty ones are beaten down, and are fled apace, and look not back: for fear was round about, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set this collection beside its predecessors, noting that in one earlier prophet the oracles on six neighbouring peoples only clear the ground for judgment on Judah, teaching that the world opposed to God must be judged before his kingdom advances, while in another the governing thought is that every apostate kingdom shall be humbled and driven to take refuge with the God of Israel; they also reason from the prophet's station in the later vision. Ellicott sees traces of a plan in the arrangement, the pieces concerned only with outside nations collected as an appendix and most of them developing what an earlier chapter gave in outline, and identifies the Egyptian king as the last of the great native sovereigns, sixth of his dynasty and sixteen years on the throne, while leaving the site of the disputed fortress open.

Gill prefers concerning the nations to against them and notes that the oracles are uniformly against, never in favour, says Egypt comes first because its overthrow came first and because the Jews had leaned on it heavily, distinguishes the greater shield from the horseman's lighter buckler, and thinks the muster addressed to the Egyptian army rather than the Chaldean and spoken by God, who bids them do their utmost and come to nothing; Calvin holds that the volume was formed without the sequence of time being kept, these threats having been uttered long before, supplies the alliances behind the campaign, explains that prophets do not narrate but stage the scene and lend their voice to other persons, here to the Egyptian king's crier, notes that chariots were then the manner of fighting, and gives the reason for the reversal, that judged by outward splendour the army must have been reckoned victorious, but the prophet is set on a watch-tower, from which what looked formidable is frail.

Clarke divides the chapter into two prophecies, one before the engagement in which the Egyptians were routed and the other belonging to an invasion long after the fall of Jerusalem, remarks that these chapters far excel what precedes them in majesty and elegance, traces the campaign from the death of the good king through the taking and garrisoning of the fortress to its recapture with immense slaughter, derives the verb for polishing from the French, describes the armour as overlapping scales, and presses the incongruity of so well-appointed a force panic-struck with its commanders beaten down while rallying it; Wesley makes the opening line the heading of all that follows to the end but one, and calls the armour simply coats of mail.

Henry states the principle that God is King and Judge of nations and will call to account those who take no notice of him, sets the word of the Lord against the Gentiles here beside the word for them in the later covenant, holds that Egypt comes first as Israel's old oppressors and late deceivers, and explains why a man already in Babylon is shown the fate of a distant army, since captives reckoned their own peace and trouble by such events.

debates.question: What does the arrangement of these foreign-nation oracles show?

positions.position: Traces of a plan: pieces concerned only with outside nations were collected as an appendix, most developing what an earlier chapter gave in outline.
Only that the volume was formed without the sequence of time being kept; the threats were uttered long before they were gathered.
That the opening line is a title for everything that follows to the end but one.

debates.question: Who is being told to muster for battle?

positions.position: The Egyptian army, and the command comes from God, who bids them do their utmost and come to nothing.
The prophet takes the part of the Egyptian king's own crier, staging the scene rather than narrating it.
It is simply the summons to a general armament.

outliers.claim: Sets the word of the Lord against the Gentiles here beside the word of the Lord for them in the later covenant, making the pair the point of the whole collection.

Reads the collection against two earlier prophets, in one of whom the foreign oracles merely clear the ground for judgment on Judah, and in the other press every apostate kingdom toward refuge with the God of Israel.

themes: The word of the Lord which came to Jeremiah the prophet against the Gentiles;

Against Egypt, against the army of Pharaoh–necho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah.
Order ye the buckler and shield, and draw near to battle.
Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen, and stand forth with your helmets; furbish the spears, and put on the brigandines.
Wherefore have I seen them dismayed and turned away back? and their mighty ones are beaten down, and are fled apace, and look not back: for fear was round about, saith the Lord.

6.pericope_label: Let not the swift flee away, nor the mighty man escape; they shall stumble, and fall toward the north by the river Euphrates. Who is this that cometh up as a flood, whose waters are moved as the rivers? Egypt riseth up like a flood, and his waters are moved like the rivers; and he saith, I will go up, and will cover the earth; I will destroy the city and the inhabitants thereof. Come up, ye horses; and rage, ye chariots; and let the mighty men come forth; the Ethiopians and the Libyans, that handle the shield; and the Lydians, that handle and bend the bow. For this is the day of the Lord God of hosts, a day of vengeance, that he may avenge him of his adversaries: and the sword shall devour, and it shall be satiate and made drunk with their blood: for the Lord God of hosts hath a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates. Go up into Gilead, and take balm, O virgin, the daughter of Egypt: in vain shalt thou use many medicines; for thou shalt not be cured. The nations have heard of thy shame, and thy cry hath filled the land: for the mighty man hath stumbled against the mighty, and they are fallen both together.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch treat the astonished question about the flood as one that gets its own answer, the hosts covering the land like that river's waves, read the muster of allies as before, let the host approach and perish nonetheless, argue from the parallelism that the horses are told to prance rather than to be mounted, supply the ground of the vengeance in Egypt's offences against the people of God, not merely of late in killing their king, carrying off one successor and making a vassal of the next, but from the earliest times, press the title virgin as a people not hitherto forced and now violated, and render the closing stumble as hero against hero, one over another in confused flight; Ellicott, borrowing the language of earlier prophets, makes Egypt the victim of a great sacrifice and the river bank the altar, identifies the auxiliaries as the peoples of the upper valley and an African people named everywhere as ally or tributary of Egypt, hears triumphant irony in the counsel to seek balm, notes that the balm passed for a cure of all wounds, and finds a second sarcasm in the title virgin.

Gill gives both readings of the line about the swift, a prohibition and a flat future, and prefers the second, draws the flood figure from the annual overflow and finds in it numbers, noise, and force threatening to carry all before it, takes the call to horses and chariots as God's ironical bidding, says the day would be not theirs but the Lord's, who commands every army, and notes the region's fame for its healing gum; Calvin allows that the particle is often prohibitive but judges the future more consistent, notes that the prophets habitually call the Chaldeans northerners even when Egyptians are addressed, explains that the astonished question is put according to the common judgment of men and meets the doubt of the godly who reckon strongholds a security, observes that this king triumphed before he fought, fastens the vengeance on the killing of the good king and finds consolation for the chosen people in the naming of Egypt as God's adversary, limits the ruin carefully, since the nation did not perish though the kingdom kept within its borders and brought out its forces no more, and explains why the report would travel, a small loss going unnoticed where one decisive engagement is proclaimed everywhere.

Clarke says that not even the swiftest shall escape, compares the advancing army to a river swollen in harvest and calls it a fine image for the incursion of vast armies, takes the first auxiliary name for the Arabs bordering Egypt near the eastern sea and the second for Libyans while reporting a contention that the third were bowmen, sees in the day of the Lord a mighty sacrifice with innumerable victims, and calls the counsel to seek balm an irony and the wound incurable, the figure the more pointed because the Egyptians were long celebrated for medicine; Wesley fixes the stumbling at the fortress by the river, reduces the drunken sword to a figure for slaughter, and agrees that in the rout those in front and those behind went down together.

debates.question: Who are the auxiliaries in the Egyptian army?

positions.position: The Arabs bordering Egypt near the eastern sea, then Libyans, with a contention that the third people were bowmen.
The peoples of the upper valley, at times independent and now subject, and an African people named everywhere as ally or tributary of Egypt.
The point of the catalogue is not identification but incredibility: hired troops from every quarter made the prophecy hard to believe.

debates.question: In what sense is the battle a day of the Lord?

positions.position: It would be not their day but the Lord's, who commands every army.
A mighty sacrifice with innumerable victims.
A great sacrifice in which Egypt is the victim and the river bank the altar.
A day of vengeance grounded in offences against the people of God reaching back to the earliest times, not only the recent ones.

outliers.claim: Says the astonished question exists to meet the doubt of the godly, who reckon strongholds a security and so leave the power of God out of account.
Sharpens the irony of the balm by noting that the Egyptians had been celebrated for medicine longer than almost any people.

themes: Let not the swift flee away, nor the mighty man escape; they shall stumble, and fall toward the north by the river Euphrates.
Who is this that cometh up as a flood, whose waters are moved as the rivers?
Egypt riseth up like a flood, and his waters are moved like the rivers; and he saith, I will go up, and will cover the earth; I will destroy the city and the inhabitants thereof.
Come up, ye horses; and rage, ye chariots; and let the mighty men come forth; the Ethiopians and the Libyans, that handle the shield; and the Lydians, that handle and bend the bow.

For this is the day of the Lord God of hosts, a day of vengeance, that he may avenge him of his adversaries: and the sword shall devour, and it shall be satiate and made drunk with their blood: for the Lord God of hosts hath a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates.
Go up into Gilead, and take balm, O virgin, the daughter of Egypt: in vain shalt thou use many medicines; for thou shalt not be cured.
The nations have heard of thy shame, and thy cry hath filled the land: for the mighty man hath stumbled against the mighty, and they are fallen both together.

13.pericope_label: The word that the Lord spake to Jeremiah the prophet, how Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon should come and smite the land of Egypt. Declare ye in Egypt, and publish in Migdol, and publish in Noph and in Tahpanhes: say ye, Stand fast, and prepare thee; for the sword shall devour round about thee. Why are thy valiant men swept away? they stood not, because the Lord did drive them. He made many to fall, yea, one fell upon another: and they said, Arise, and let us go again to our own people, and to the land of our nativity, from the oppressing sword. They did cry there, Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise; he hath passed the time appointed.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch notice an unusual formula in the heading and suggest the piece was never uttered publicly, only written down, see the power of Egypt already broken in spirit, note that the disputed noun elsewhere describes stallions and bulls and weigh whether men of war are meant since the singular verbs point to a singular noun the form resists, leave the speakers of the flight indefinite and take them for strangers generally rather than hired troops or allied nations, fix the place of the closing cry as Egypt itself, argue that its noun means ruin rather than noise, and record the variant reading name for there while dismissing one rendering built on it as decidedly false; Ellicott agrees the second oracle is distinct and thinks it delivered much later, says the general summons is narrowed to the invader's immediate objects, cuts the knot of the disputed line by reading thy strong bull dragged away, which the old versions support in number and the Greek refers to the sacred bull that stood for the chief deity, thinks of settlers an earlier king had encouraged or refugees from Judah, records a Greek text that made the oppressing sword a Grecian one, and prefers a slightly altered text giving they have called the name of Pharaoh, A Noise, he has let the appointed season pass.

Gill distinguishes the two oracles by scope, the first concerning an army overthrown at one place and this the destruction of the land some years later, dated by a rabbinic chronicle to the twenty-seventh year of the Babylonian's reign, takes the proclamation as notice of the invader's coming, derives the verb of sweeping from a torrent and applies it to the force driving men from their posts, and assigns the closing cry to the auxiliaries in the field rather than to mocking Chaldeans or Egyptians complaining at home; Calvin gives the reason for a second visitation, that Egypt was punished not only for provoking God but for corrupting the Jews, and that the word came while both were still secure, rejects identifying the second city with the great port and denies it can be the first since the prophet lists them separately, defends the forcible style against plain statement, lets the astonishment stand as rhetoric since unbelievers treat prophecy as fable and sleep over their prosperity, supplies God as the unnamed subject of the stumbling and observes that crowding alone would do the work, and hears in the cry soldiers who had believed the boasting, come to Pharaoh as to a god and finding a king of tumult.

Clarke supplies the Greek equivalents of the three named cities and reads the sword devouring round about of neighbouring peoples already flattened by Chaldean arms, has ranks falling on ranks in terror with the fugitives being the auxiliaries, and prints a version of the closing cry in which the allies excuse themselves to their king because a tumult prevented the appointed meeting; Wesley keeps it simple, a great noise that came to nothing and a day the king fixed himself and let slip.
Henry states the justice of the second visitation plainly: those who encroached on others should be encroached on themselves.

debates.question: What is the strong one that is swept away?

positions.position: The valiant men, swept off as by a torrent when the invading force drove them from their posts.
Probably the men of war, though the singular verbs and suffix point awkwardly to a singular noun the form resists.
Thy strong bull dragged away: the sacred bull that stood for the chief deity, so that the line is the triumph of Israel's God over an animal god.

debates.question: How should the cry about Pharaoh be read?

positions.position: The noun means ruin, not noise, and the crying happens in Egypt, where one falls over another.
A slightly altered text is best: they have called the name of Pharaoh, A Noise; he has let the appointed season pass.
It is the allies excusing themselves to their king, a tumult having prevented the appointed meeting.
A great noise that came to nothing, and a day the king had fixed himself and let slip.

outliers.claim: Defends the forcible prophetic manner against plain statement, since unlike public speakers courting applause the prophets meant to teach and threaten to some effect.
Infers from the unusual heading formula that this prophecy may never have been delivered aloud, only written down.

themes: The word that the Lord spake to Jeremiah the prophet, how Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon should come and smite the land of Egypt.
Declare ye in Egypt, and publish in Migdol, and publish in Noph and in Tahpanhes: say ye, Stand fast, and prepare thee; for the sword shall devour round about thee.
Why are thy valiant men swept away? they stood not, because the Lord did drive them.
He made many to fall, yea, one fell upon another: and they said, Arise, and let us go again to our own people, and to the land of our nativity, from the oppressing sword.
They did cry there, Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise; he hath passed the time appointed.

18.pericope_label: As I live, saith the King, whose name is the Lord of hosts, Surely as Tabor is among the mountains, and as Carmel by the sea, so shall he come. O thou daughter dwelling in Egypt, furnish thyself to go into captivity: for Noph shall be waste and desolate without an inhabitant. Egypt is like a very fair heifer, but destruction cometh; it cometh out of the north. Also her hired men are in the midst of her like fatted bullocks; for they also are turned back, and are fled away together: they did not stand, because the day of their calamity was come upon them, and the time of their visitation. The voice thereof shall go like a serpent; for they shall march with an army, and come against her with axes, as hewers of wood. They shall cut down her forest, saith the Lord, though it cannot be searched; because they are more than the grasshoppers, and are innumerable.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note the feminine of the heifer chosen to match the personified nation and read the adjective as very beautiful rather than coquetting, the beast being a people well fed in a rich land, observe that the rare word for what comes from the north points to pinching or nipping and so yields a stinging fly rather than plain destruction, distinguish the mercenaries from the allies named earlier and explain the comparison by the camps where the crown kept them well provided since it depended on them, and call the clause about the serpent's voice difficult while rejecting the emendation that turns its verb into hissing; Ellicott takes the two mountains for the invader in his high-towering greatness, one rising in solitary bulk above the plain and the other above the sea, has the personified nation preparing with the instruments of captivity and the old capital left depopulated, makes the gadfly sting the heifer into the madness of agony while noting that the image points at the animal worship and recalling the Greek legend of a girl turned into a heifer and so tormented, makes the mercenaries a drove of terrified cattle driven to the slaughter-house, and has the serpent hissing in rage in the forest the enemy is entering before the sign gives way to barbarous tribes with axes instead of swords.

Gill weighs the divine title behind the oath, a king greater than either of the two named, who swears by his own life because there is nothing greater, pictures inhabitants long settled in security, reads the heifer as never yoked because never conquered and fat enough for slaughter, has the mercenaries as foreigners who lived so deliciously they were unfit for war while reporting the reading that makes them the princes in charge of the heifer, and contrasts the bellowing of a heifer in fat pasture with the hiss of a serpent driven from its hole, taking the voice for submission and citing the ancients for the thinness of that sound while reporting a reading that hears the serpents from far off; Calvin explains why an oath was needed, since delay had persuaded the Egyptians the threat was false or forgotten while the Jews had their own dismissals, says God suspends punishment and the vengeance breaks out when the unbelieving least expect it, makes the order to pack deliberate provocation since the unbelieving stay stupid unless their torpor is shaken out by force, notes that the city sentenced to solitude was the one whose monuments were counted among the wonders of the world, says abundance is named because it blinds, observes that hired men look the more warlike but that soft living ruins soldiers, agrees the complaint would be no clamour but a mutter, and renders the difficult clause as saying the forest cannot be searched out.

Clarke, describing the first mountain as standing alone and highest in its neighbourhood, turns the comparison round, so that were the Egyptians as distinguished for valour as those hills for height they still could not stand the coming shock, says of the order to pack only that the thing is unavoidable, and numbers the cities of the forest at one thousand and twenty; Wesley takes the mountains a third way, of encompassing, since the enemy will surround them as surely as one hill is ringed by mountains and the other by the sea, reads the axes as a felling of woodland, and glosses the difficult clause as impenetrable.

debates.question: What do the two mountains in the oath illustrate?

positions.position: The invader in his high-towering greatness, one hill rising in solitary bulk above the plain and the other above the sea.
Egypt's own valour: were the Egyptians as distinguished for it as those hills for height, they still could not stand the shock.
Encompassing: the enemy will surround them as surely as one hill is ringed by mountains and the other by the sea.

debates.question: What does the heifer figure carry?

positions.position: A beast never yoked because the nation was never conquered, and fat enough for slaughter.
A people carefully and abundantly fed in a rich land, the feminine chosen to match the personified nation.
A pointed reference to the animal worship, the nation being like its god, with a gadfly to sting it into the madness of agony.
A warning that abundance blinds, which is why the prophets name the wealth of the ungodly at all.

outliers.claim: Notes the irony that the city sentenced to stand empty was the one whose monuments were counted among the wonders of the world.
Finds a striking parallel in the Greek legend of a girl turned into a heifer and driven from land to land by a gadfly.

themes: As I live, saith the King, whose name is the Lord of hosts, Surely as Tabor is among the mountains, and as Carmel by the sea, so shall he come.
O thou daughter dwelling in Egypt, furnish thyself to go into captivity: for Noph shall be waste and desolate without an inhabitant.
Egypt is like a very fair heifer, but destruction cometh; it cometh out of the north.

Also her hired men are in the midst of her like fatted bullocks; for they also are turned back, and are fled away together: they did not stand, because the day of their calamity was come upon them, and the time of their visitation.
The voice thereof shall go like a serpent; for they shall march with an army, and come against her with axes, as hewers of wood.
They shall cut down her forest, saith the Lord, though it cannot be searched; because they are more than the grasshoppers, and are innumerable.

24.pericope_label: The daughter of Egypt shall be confounded; she shall be delivered into the hand of the people of the north. The Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, saith; Behold, I will punish the multitude of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, with their gods, and their kings; even Pharaoh, and all them that trust in him: And I will deliver them into the hand of those that seek their lives, and into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of his servants: and afterward it shall be inhabited, as in the days of old, saith the Lord. But fear not thou, O my servant Jacob, and be not dismayed, O Israel: for, behold, I will save thee from afar off, and thy seed from the land of their captivity; and Jacob shall return, and be in rest and at ease, and none shall make him afraid. Fear thou not, O Jacob my servant, saith the Lord: for I am with thee; for I will make a full end of all the nations whither I have driven thee: but I will not make a full end of thee, but correct thee in measure; yet will I not leave thee wholly unpunished.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark the closing verses off as a promise addressed to Israel rather than a continuation of the sentence on Egypt; Ellicott reads the punishment of the god as Amon of No, taking the first word as the deity's name with a play on its Hebrew sense of multitude and putting the city in the south, and hears in the promise of reinhabiting the gleam of hope that ends other visions of judgment, while stating the limit exactly: Egypt was to revive, but never again to stand among the conquerors of the world.

Gill has the kingdom, or its people, shamed before all nations and carried away, reports the rabbinic explanation of the divine title as God of Israel here, that the vengeance repaid the treatment of Israel by two of its kings, takes the sufferers of the delivering up to be the king, his people and all who trusted him, and reads the closing repetition as consolation against the fear of being cast off, with the divine presence promised to men still far off in captivity; Calvin adds the tone of the conquest, that the victors would be proud and treat the beaten reproachfully, explains the repetition by the incredibility of the thing and the settled unbelief the prophet was contending with, takes the disputed word in its Hebrew sense and puts the city at the port later renamed after its Macedonian founder, presses that to seek a life is exactly not to spare it and that naming the servants as well as the king degrades further, treats the restoration as no favour to a heathen nation but proof that God would not destroy it utterly while noting that another prophet makes the restored kingdom small and abject, explains why a promise to Israel belongs at the end of an oracle about foreigners, and says the repetition was needed because captivity was little short of death, the promise resting on gratuitous adoption alone.

Clarke identifies the people of the north as the Chaldeans, reads the punished god as the Egyptian name of their chief deity whose temple stood in the city the Greeks called after their own Zeus, the Thebes famous for a hundred gates, reports the promise of reinhabiting as fulfilled within forty years on a contemporary's authority, and reads the closing promise in the light of what followed, the city taken, the temple burnt, the people carried off and a seed still preserved, quoting a writer who calls the survival of that people among the ruins of all their conquerors one of the most illustrious acts of providence, since raindrops and rivers alike are lost in the sea while this people flowed into every part of the world, mixed with all nations, and stayed separate from them all.

Henry states the purpose of the closing verses in a sentence, that comfort and peace are spoken to the Israel of God while judgment is abroad among the nations, and sets out the two halves of the comparison that ends the chapter, correction in measure on one side and no everlasting destruction on the other.

debates.question: Which city is meant by the place of the punished god?

positions.position: Thebes, famous for its hundred gates, where the great temple of the chief Egyptian god stood.
The southern capital, the name being the god's with a play on its Hebrew sense of multitude.
The word is simply the Hebrew for multitude, and the city is the northern port later renamed after its Macedonian founder; in any case a part stands for the whole country.

debates.question: How far does the promise of Egypt's revival reach?

positions.position: It was fulfilled within forty years, on the authority of a contemporary prophet.
Egypt was to revive, but never again to stand among the conquerors and tyrants of the world.
Not favour to a heathen nation but proof that God would not destroy it utterly; another prophet makes the restored kingdom small and abject where this one seems to promise the old prosperity.

outliers.claim: Quotes at length a writer who makes the survival of the Jews among the ruins of all their conquerors one of the most illustrious acts of providence, since raindrops and rivers alike are lost in the sea while this people mixed with all nations and stayed separate from them.
Explains that the prophet was never appointed a teacher of the nations, so that everything said about foreign peoples was said for the benefit of his own.

themes: The daughter of Egypt shall be confounded; she shall be delivered into the hand of the people of the north.
The Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, saith; Behold, I will punish the multitude of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, with their gods, and their kings; even Pharaoh, and all them that trust in him:

And I will deliver them into the hand of those that seek their lives, and into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of his servants: and afterward it shall be inhabited, as in the days of old, saith the Lord.

But fear not thou, O my servant Jacob, and be not dismayed, O Israel: for, behold, I will save thee from afar off, and thy seed from the land of their captivity; and Jacob shall return, and be in rest and at ease, and none shall make him afraid.

Fear thou not, O Jacob my servant, saith the Lord: for I am with thee; for I will make a full end of all the nations whither I have driven thee: but I will not make a full end of thee, but correct thee in measure; yet will I not leave thee wholly unpunished.
